Hard Problems and Randomized Algorithms

Some problems have no known fast method. See why checking an answer can be easy while finding one is hard, carry hardness from one problem to another with reductions, get answers with a guarantee from approximation, and let dice make algorithms fast on average.

Part 1

🔐P and NP: easy to check, hard to find

Some problems have fast methods, like sorting or shortest paths. Computer scientists call this class P: problems solvable in polynomial time, such as n² or n³ steps. Other problems are only known to be fast to check. Given a proposed answer, you can confirm it quickly, but nobody knows how to find one quickly. That class is NP. Subset sum is a classic example: does some group of the numbers add up to the target?

NameMeaning
PCan be solved in polynomial time
NPA proposed answer can be checked in polynomial time
NP-hardAt least as hard as every problem in NP
NP-completeIn NP and NP-hard, such as SAT, subset sum, vertex cover and Hamiltonian path
Whether P equals NP is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems of the Clay Mathematics Institute, with a prize of one million dollars. Most researchers believe P is not equal to NP, but nobody has proved it.
Dynamic programming 2 solved subset sum in about n × target steps. That is only fast when the target is small, because the target can have many digits, and each extra digit multiplies the work by 10.
Part 2

🔁Reductions: one problem dressed as another

A reduction rewrites one problem as another, so a solver for the second also solves the first. Here is a tiny one. An independent set is a group of vertices with no edge between any two of them. A vertex cover is a group of vertices that touches every edge. Take the vertices left out of an independent set, and you always get a vertex cover.

largest independent set + smallest vertex cover = number of vertices
In 1971 Stephen Cook proved that SAT is NP-complete, and Leonid Levin found the same result on his own. In 1972 Richard Karp used reductions to show that 21 well known problems, including vertex cover, are NP-complete too.
Direction matters. To show a new problem is hard, reduce a known hard problem to it. Reducing the new problem to a hard one only shows that the new one is no harder.
Part 3

🎯Approximation: good enough, with a guarantee

When the exact answer is out of reach, an approximation algorithm runs fast and promises to land within a fixed factor of the best answer. For vertex cover the method is short: walk through the edges, and whenever an edge has no chosen end yet, take both of its ends.

Here is the reason for the factor 2. The edges we took both ends of share no vertex. Any cover, even the best one, needs at least one end of each of them. So the best cover has at least as many vertices as we took edges, and we chose exactly two per edge.
ProblemA known guarantee
Vertex cover2, by taking both ends
Travelling salesman, when no detour is shorter than the direct road1.5, by Christofides' method
Set coverabout ln n, by greedy
Knapsackas close to 1 as you like, with more time
Part 4

🎲Randomized algorithms: quickselect

A randomized algorithm rolls dice while it runs. Quickselect finds the k-th smallest value without sorting. It picks a random pivot, splits the range around it like quicksort, and then keeps only the side that holds the answer. A bad pivot can happen, but random pivots make a long run of bad ones very unlikely.

expected work ≈ n + n ÷ 2 + n ÷ 4 + … < 2n, so O(n) on average
KindAnswerRunning timeExample
Las VegasAlways rightRandomQuickselect, quicksort
Monte CarloProbably rightFixedMiller-Rabin prime test, estimating π
The median of medians method picks a pivot that is always good enough, so it runs in O(n) even in the worst case. It is slower in practice, which is why libraries usually choose random pivots.
Part 5

🌊Reservoir sampling and Monte Carlo

Reservoir sampling picks k items fairly from a stream whose length is unknown, using only k slots. Keep the first k items. When item number i arrives, keep it with chance k ÷ i, in place of a random kept item. Every item ends with the same chance, k ÷ n.

A Monte Carlo method uses many random tries to estimate a number. Throw random points into a square and count how many land inside the quarter circle. That share is close to π ÷ 4.

π ≈ 4 × points inside ÷ all points    error shrinks like 1 ÷ √N
To make an estimate 10 times more accurate, a Monte Carlo method needs about 100 times as many points. Our run of 10000 points gave 3.1352, close to π but not exact.
